topic: Yale David Geffen School of Drama Acting program coursework, policies, and facilities, 2026-2027

findings.value: This is a studio-based exploration of the internal and external preparation an actor must undergo in order to effectively render the moment-to-moment life of a given character. ... The first term of this class employs a series of questions to examine the principles and craft behind acting technique while exploring the plays of a wide variety of twentieth- and twenty-first-century playwrights. The second term includes a sequence of simulated rehearsals in order to put those principles and craft into practice.
findings.source: https://bulletin.yale.edu/sites/default/files/david-geffen-school-of-drama-2026-2027.pdf (David Geffen School of Drama Bulletin 2026-2027, Acting (M.F.A. and Certificate), Courses of Instruction)
findings.quote: DRAM 103a/b, Acting I This is a studio-based exploration of the internal and external preparation an actor must undergo in order to effectively render the moment-to-moment life of a given character. This course is meant to promote a rigorous investigation of how the actor uses the self as the foundation for transformation. The first term of this class employs a series of questions to examine the principles and craft behind acting technique while exploring the plays of a wide variety of twentieth- and twenty-first-century playwrights. The second term includes a sequence of simulated rehearsals in order to put those principles and craft into practice. Gregory Wallace

findings.value: First-year voice training is a progression of exercises/experiences to liberate the natural voice from habitual tensions, connect image/intention/emotion to breath and sound, and develop vocal expression, ease, clarity, power, stamina, range, and sensitivity to impulse.
findings.quote: DRAM 113a/b, Voice I The first year of voice training is structured as a progression of exercises/experiences designed to liberate the individual's natural voice from habitual psychophysical tensions; to connect image, intention, and emotion to breath and sound; to develop the voice's potential for expression and awaken the actor's appetite for language; and to promote vocal ease, clarity, power, stamina, range, and sensitivity to impulse. Walton Wilson

findings.what: DRAM 123a/b Speech and Accents I: description
findings.value: Speech training broadens the actor's range of imaginative vocal expression and deepens sensory relationship to language; actors examine their own speech habits/idiolects, build accent-transformation tools (vocal tract posture, prosody, phonetics), and in term two study accents in connection with dramatic text.
findings.quote: DRAM 123a/b, Speech and Accents I Speech training seeks to broaden the actor's range of imaginative vocal expression and to deepen the actor's sensory relationship to language. Actors conduct a rigorous examination of their own speech habits, idiolects, and linguistic identity through exploration of vocal physiology. Through this examination of their own idiolects, actors build the tools of accent transformation, including vocal tract posture, prosody (melody and rhythm), and phonetics. To encourage speech that flows freely from impulse and breath, the approach uses exercises that are actively rooted in the whole body rather than being limited to the surfaces of the mouth. In the second term, the actors broaden the boundaries of their language use through the study of accents in connection with dramatic text, including texts used in acting classes. Julie Foh

findings.what: DRAM 133a/b The Body as Source I: description
findings.value: Works to bring awareness and integration to the physical, mental, emotional, and energetic aspects of the actor via physical training exercises; includes application to character creation and a body-first approach to scene-work.
findings.quote: DRAM 133a/b, The Body as Source I This course works to bring awareness and integration to the physical, mental, emotional, and energetic aspects of the actor. Through specific physical training exercises, participants are encouraged to identify and release holdings in the mind/body system, allowing them to deepen a connection to imagery, physical impulses, and acting choices. The class also includes application to character creation and a body-first approach to scene-work. Erica Fae

findings.value: Offered in all three years through class work and private tutorials; develops kinesthetic/spatial awareness, balance, alignment, and the breath-based connection between voice and body.
findings.quote: DRAM 143a/b, Alexander Technique I Offered in all three years through class work and private tutorials, this work develops the actor's kinesthetic and spatial awareness, fosters balance and alignment, and, through breath work, promotes the connection between voice and body. Fabio Tavares

findings.value: Explores the actor's playful spirit and the theatrical event as 'game' through games, improvisation and composition exercises; exercises explore status, focus, scale, presence, flow, and impulse, delving into 'le jeu,' the actor's pleasure in playing.
findings.quote: DRAM 153a, Play This course explores the actor's playful spirit and the notion of the theatrical event as "game." Through a series of games and improvisation and composition exercises, students develop complicity with fellow actors/the audience and discover qualities of openness, spontaneity, generosity, and attack as they are encouraged to take risks, access their imagination, and play fully with their voice and body. Exercises explore status, focus, scale, presence, flow, and impulse while delving into the mysterious nature of "le jeu," the actor's pleasure in playing. Justine Williams

findings.what: DRAM 163b Text Analysis I (The Actor's Table Work): description
findings.value: Inspired by Katie Mitchell's method; first-year actors mine the facts/questions in a text's given circumstances, start with table work on one text, then move into working on their feet in the second half of the course.
findings.quote: DRAM 163b, Text Analysis I: The Actor's Table Work Inspired by Katie Mitchell's method of text analysis, first-year Acting students mine the facts and questions embedded in the text of a play in order to build a full sensory-driven, stakes-enlivened embodiment of character and given circumstances. By providing first-year actors with tools for close reading, physical embodiment, and the activation of language, this course seeks to help students identify and activate what is given on the page, what is theirs to author. Actors start work around the table on one text practicing the "actor's table work" and move into working on their feet towards the second half of the course. Tamilla Woodard

findings.what: DRAM 403a/b Acting Intimacy and Combat for the Stage: description
findings.value: Provides first-year actors an understanding of techniques and safety measures for theatrical violence and intimacy; term one covers consent and intimacy work integrated into scene life, term two covers physicalizing conflict and violence through individual, partner, and group exploration, exercises, scene work, and performance.
findings.quote: DRAM 403a/b, Acting Intimacy and Combat for the Stage This course is designed to provide the first-year actor with an understanding of the techniques and safety measures employed in the practice of theatrical violence and intimacy and how to fully embody them in character. In the first term we investigate the process for consent and intimacy work and how to integrate them into the moment-to-moment life of a scene. In the second term we focus on physicalizing conflict and violence. We do so through individual, partner, and group physical exploration, exercises, scene work, and performance. This course fosters the understanding of collaboration, consent, organic response, and a deeper knowledge of the physical self and the group dynamic. Kelsey Rainwater, Michael Rossmy

findings.what: DRAM 873a/b Text and Context Across the Repertory: description
findings.value: Explores strategies for mining theatrical texts through attention to multiple contexts, drawing on the current Yale Rep season; includes lectures, discussion, digressions, weekly reading assignments, spontaneous research, occasional written assignments, and in-class presentations.
findings.quote: DRAM 873a/b, Text and Context Across the Repertory A text, a space, an actor, an audience: since earliest times these have served as the building blocks of theatrical performance. Each is ripe with possibilities informed by the social, cultural, political, economic, and historical contexts that have shaped it. Focusing on the collaboration between text and context and drawing examples from the current season of plays at Yale Repertory Theater and beyond, this course explores strategies for mining theatrical texts through attention to the multiple contexts with which that text is in conversation. It celebrates curiosity, embraces obsessions, and encourages the free flow of the imagination. It includes lectures, discussion, digressions, weekly reading assignments, spontaneous research, occasional written assignments, and in-class presentations. Spring semester continues reading plays beyond the rep season, extending the exploration of text and performance. Paul Walsh and Faculty.

findings.what: DRAM 163a Text Analysis II (second year): description
findings.value: Second-year course giving tools to mine the printed text for given circumstances, character, objective, and action, promoting the actor as interpretive artist.
findings.quote: DRAM 163a, Text Analysis II This course seeks to provide second-year Acting students with tools to mine the printed text for given circumstances, character, objective, and action, noting the opportunities and limitations that the printed play script presents and promoting the freedom and responsibility of the actor as an interpretive artist. James Bundy

findings.what: DRAM 203a/b Acting II: Plays of Extended and Heightened Language: description
findings.value: Second-year actors and directors tackle Shakespeare's language (fall) and heightened language from a range of playwrights 16th-20th century (spring) through studio-based scene work, with tutorials augmenting classwork.
findings.quote: DRAM 203a, Acting II: Plays of Extended and Heightened Language ... The course begins by drawing actors and directors onto the same page regarding the technical elements of Shakespeare's language and quickly moves to the actor's craft and process and an exploration of Shakespeare's events and characters through studio-based scene work. ... Material for the course is taken from scenes, speeches, and other set texts of Shakespeare. Tutorials are scheduled to augment classwork. Mary Lou Rosato / DRAM 203b ... The course is composed of studio-based scene work, and actors continue to make use of the myriad of tools that have been in development in the previous three semesters. Mary Lou Rosato

findings.value: Deepens awareness of voice as kinesthetic experience; develops ability to embody text through continued physical release work, discovery of resonant spaces, and advanced vocal skills along with visceral and imaginative text exploration.
findings.quote: DRAM 213a/b, Voice II (Class and Tutorials) In the second year of voice training, students focus on deepening their awareness of voice as a kinesthetic experience rooted in the body and the need for expression. Voice II explores how to meet the demands of text with clarity, emotional depth, personal connection, generosity of scale, ease, and healthy habits. The actor develops the ability to embody the text through continued physical release work, discovery of resonant spaces, and advanced vocal skills along with visceral and imaginative text exploration. Walton Wilson, Grace Zandarski

findings.what: DRAM 223a/b Speech and Accents II: description
findings.value: Expands the actor's vocal and imaginative range beyond own idiolect, applied to heightened dramatic texts; second term offers intensive study of accents and dialects for character transformation and integrative performances.
findings.quote: DRAM 223a/b, Speech and Accents II The second year of speech training continues to expand the actor's range of vocal and imaginative expression away from their own idiolect to expand the actor's toolbox and deepen sensory relationship to language as applied to heightened dramatic texts. In the second term, this course offers an intensive study of accents and dialects to provide multiple opportunities for the experience of character transformation and embodying the work into integrative performances. Amanda Quaid

findings.what: DRAM 233a/b The Body as Source II: description
findings.value: Continues year-one work, deepening training of the energetic body and connection to imagery/impulses while navigating text demands; students take on a solo piece of 'physical scoring' culminating in a showing for the community.
findings.quote: DRAM 233a/b, The Body as Source II This course continues the work of year one, deepening the training of the energetic body and the connection to imagery and physical impulses while navigating the demands of text. We then carve into the work of "physical scoring" by taking on a solo piece that culminates in a showing for the community. Erica Fae

findings.what: DRAM 243a/b Alexander Technique II Tutorials: description
findings.value: Develops kinesthetic awareness, balance, alignment, movement coordination, and the mind-voice-body connection through breath work, applied during rehearsal and performance.
findings.quote: DRAM 243a/b, Alexander Technique II Tutorials This work develops the actor's kinesthetic awareness; fosters balance and alignment; coordinates movement; and, through breath work, promotes the connection between mind, voice, and body. All these elements are applied during rehearsal and performance. Through clarity of intention, the actor can find the organic physical life of the character. Bill Connington

findings.value: Focuses on discovery of the playful self through exercises in rhythm, balance, generosity, and abandon, removing blocks/filters so actors learn to play without worry and discover their personal clown.
findings.quote: DRAM 263a/b, Clown This course focuses on the discovery of the playful self through exercises in rhythm, balance, generosity, and abandon. The blocks and filters that prevent the actor from following impulses fully are removed. It allows the actor to listen with the body and begin to give more value to the pleasure of performance. Once actors learn to play without worry, they begin to discover the personal clown that lives in the center of the comic world. Annelise Lawson, Chris Bayes

findings.value: A practice of movement as invention through improvisation, physical research, phrase work, and composition; solo, duet, and ensemble work build toward kinetic specificity and collective listening.
findings.quote: DRAM 273a, Movement Invention II This course is a practice of movement as invention. Through improvisation, physical research, phrase work, and composition, participants develop deep artistic agency, cultivating alignment between impulse and gesture, presence and intention, personal expression and form. The class moves through studies on imagery, effort, form, space, relationship, habit, musicality, and narrative. Solo, duet, and ensemble work build toward a practice rooted in kinetic specificity and collective listening. Andrea Miller

findings.value: Second-year scene study continuing to develop embodiment of heightened circumstances and poetic text, centered on scenes from classical Greek texts in translation and/or modern poetic adaptations; students prepare and rehearse scenes for presentation and exploration in class.
findings.quote: DRAM 293b, The Greeks The purpose of second-year scene study is to continue to develop the actor's ability to embody and activate heightened circumstances and poetic text. This module runs alongside the final six weeks of Plays of Extended and Heightened Language and is centered on scenes from classical Greek texts in translation and/or modern poetic adaptations. Students prepare and rehearse scenes for presentation and exploration in class. Evan Yionoulis

findings.what: DRAM 353a Play with Text (second year): description
findings.value: Returns to the actor's pleasure and principles of play, examining the actor's playful relationship to text through games, exercises, and exploits working solo, in pairs, and as a group, from improvised outbursts to established poetic or heightened texts.
findings.quote: DRAM 353a, Play with Text In the fall of second year, we return to the actor's pleasure and the principles of play as essential frameworks for coming more fully (and truthfully) to life on stage and build on these foundations to examine the actor's playful relationship to text. Through a series of games, exercises, and exploits (working solo, in pairs, and as a group), actors find ample opportunity to play with and through language--from improvised outbursts to established poetic or heightened texts. Justine Williams

findings.what: DRAM 405a/b (Advanced Principles of Acting Stage Combat, second-year continuation of 403): description
findings.value: Builds on first-year techniques, giving second-year actors understanding of armed theatrical violence techniques/safety and weapon awareness with a partner/group, then applying them through scene study and performance.
findings.quote: DRAM 405a/b, Advanced Principles of Acting Stage Combat We continue building on the techniques learned in the first year, providing the second-year actor with an understanding of the techniques and safety measures employed in the practice of armed theatrical violence. We deepen the understanding of proprioception and weapon awareness when working with a partner and within a group. Upon learning these techniques, we engage in a deeper exploration of dramatic situation and characterization through scene study and performance. Kelsey Rainwater, Michael Rossmy

findings.value: Uses tutorials and group classes to explore coordinated physical processes for a free and expressive singing voice, integrating imagination, intention, and breath with emotional/linguistic/musical demands of songs.
findings.quote: DRAM 413a/b, Singing II (Class, Tutorials) This course uses tutorials and group classes to explore the coordinated physical processes that result in a free and expressive singing voice. Through the integration of imagination, intention, and breath and the active investigation of the emotional, linguistic, and musical demands in songs, the course aims to give each student the experience of bringing healthy and expressive singing technique to bear. Glenn Seven Allen

findings.value: Director-actor collaboration lab on Shakespeare for third-year actors and second-year directors; students work together on-the-feet to unpack given circumstances, character objectives, and central dramatic conflicts.
findings.quote: DRAM 190a, Shakespeare Practicum This practicum focuses on the director-actor collaboration in rehearsals, focusing specifically on the plays of Shakespeare. In this lab, third-year actors and second-year directors learn "by doing" how to mine the form and content of a Shakespearean text. Students work together to unpack given circumstances, character objectives, and the central dramatic conflicts of scenes and plays, exploring these in on-the-feet work while negotiating the space, with the goal of strengthening their ability to make and receive offers, and to test and develop production ideas within the rehearsal process. Taught in conjunction with DRAM 120a. Karin Coonrod

findings.value: Explores classical archetypes of commedia dell'arte using mask, physical articulation, sound, and rhythm; work is primarily improvisational with the actor/creator at the center.
findings.quote: DRAM 253a, Commedia This course explores the classical archetypes of the commedia dell'arte. It makes use of mask, physical articulation, sound, and rhythm to develop the transformational power of the actors. When the mask is alive and impulses begin to travel with abandon through the physical psychology of the body, the student begins to understand the actor/audience relationship in all its ferocious beauty. The work is primarily improvisational with the actor/creator at the center of the theatrical conversation. Annelise Lawson

findings.value: Final two semesters of scene-study reinvesting in fundamentals of craft via Williams, Brecht, Valdez, Lori-Parks works; fall term includes verbatim projects embodying interview text of real persons.
findings.quote: DRAM 303a/b, Acting III This final two semesters of scene-study class reinvests in and revisits the fundamentals of the craft by engaging works that explore performance beyond the approaches of naturalism and psychological realism including the works of Tennessee Williams, Bertolt Brecht, Luis Valdez, Susan Lori-Parks. ... Running through the fall term is work on verbatim projects in which students embody and give voice to the verbatim text of persons they have interviewed, employing the fundamental tools of performance--deep and profound listening--while bringing to bear a synthesis of their vocal and physical training to date. Ron Van Lieu, Tamilla Woodard, Evan Yionoulis

findings.value: Reinforces/expands Voice II, preparing the actor to embody text and live believably in imaginary circumstances in any space/genre/size of character, with exercises extending the voice into screaming, shouting, and other vocal extremes.
findings.quote: DRAM 313a/b, Voice III (Class, Tutorials) The third-year curriculum reinforces and expands on the work of Voice II, preparing the actor to wholly embody the text and live believably in imaginary circumstances in every space, genre, and size of character. ... The course also explores exercises that extend the voice into screaming, shouting, and other vocal extremes. Walton Wilson, Grace Zandarski

findings.what: DRAM 323a/b Speech and Accents III: description
findings.value: Third-year speech training centers on the Interview Project, a deep exploration of embodying someone else's linguistic identity, culminating the application of all the actor's speech tools.
findings.quote: DRAM 323a/b, Speech and Accents III (Class, Tutorials) In the third year of speech training, actors engage in a deep exploration of embodiment of someone else's linguistic identity through the Interview Project. This course is a culmination of putting all the actors' tools into practice. Speech tutorials in the first term focus on the analysis and embodiment of other idiolects. In the second term, material for tutorials can evolve from any areas of speech, accent, and text work that the actor wishes to explore. Julie Foh, Amanda Quaid

findings.value: One-on-one sessions cultivating awareness of habits and choices in action, redirecting patterns of stress/strain over the semester to develop presence, coordination, and vitality.
findings.quote: DRAM 343a/b, Alexander Technique III (Tutorials) Alexander Technique one-on-one sessions are designed to support you and your work through cultivating awareness of habits and developing choices in action. ... As you learn to redirect patterns of stress and strain over the course of the semester, enhanced presence, balanced coordination, and dynamic vitality emerge. Eleanor Taylor

findings.what: DRAM 363a You Are the Creator: description
findings.value: Third-year actors spend their first final-year term developing their own individual performance piece (writing, singing, dancing/movement, learning an instrument, etc.) through mentoring, individual support, and small-class sections, sharing it with the Acting community at the start of second semester.
findings.quote: DRAM 363a, You Are the Creator The course offers actors the space and time during the first term of their final year of training to explore, develop, and create their own individual performance pieces. Through mentoring, individual support, and meeting in small-class sections, the actors work on a performance project of their choosing throughout the semester... This may take many creative forms... writing, singing, dancing/movement, learning a musical instrument, writing and performing music... a performance that they ultimately share with the Acting Program community at the beginning of the second semester. Joan MacIntosh

findings.what: DRAM 373a (Movement Invention III, third-year continuation of 273): description
findings.value: A practice of movement as invention through improvisation, physical research, phrase work, and composition; solo, duet, and ensemble work building toward kinetic specificity and collective listening (identical framing to the second-year course).
findings.quote: DRAM 373a, Movement Invention III This course is a practice of movement as invention. Through improvisation, physical research, phrase work, and composition, participants develop deep artistic agency, cultivating alignment between impulse and gesture, presence and intention, personal expression and form. ... Solo, duet, and ensemble work build toward a practice rooted in kinetic specificity and collective listening. Andrea Miller

findings.value: Uses tutorials and group classes focused on breath support, ease, range of expression, and clarity of storytelling, emphasizing commitment to material in performance; students required to perform in the end-of-year Singing Send-Off.
findings.quote: DRAM 423a/b, Acting Through Song (Class, Tutorials) This course uses tutorials and group classes to continue a focus on breath support, ease, range of expression, and clarity of storytelling, emphasizing the actor's commitment to the material in performance. ... Students are required to perform in the end-of-year Singing Send-Off. Lonny Price

findings.value: Three-session course where students film brief scenes of their own choice, watch and discuss them, and, when time permits, refilm them, examining their work as both listeners and talkers.
findings.quote: DRAM 463a/b, On-Camera Acting Technique This three-session course gives students experience working on camera. Brief scenes of the individual student's choice are filmed, watched, discussed, and, when time permits, filmed again. Because the camera is always on the student who has chosen the scene, they can examine their work as both listeners and talkers. Ellen Novack

findings.what: DRAM 273b Character Analysis and Movement: description
findings.value: Not found as a standalone description; the 2026-27 Bulletin's third-year table lists 'DRAM 190a Character Analysis and Movement' in the course list, but the course-of-instruction entry under DRAM 190a is titled and described only as 'Shakespeare Practicum' with no separate 'Character Analysis and Movement' description found elsewhere in the document.
findings.quote: Year Three Subject [table row] Character Analysis and Movement ... DRAM 190a Shakespeare Practicum [Plan of Study table, third-year sequence] / DRAM 190a, Shakespeare Practicum This practicum focuses on the director-actor collaboration in rehearsals, focusing specifically on the plays of Shakespeare.

findings.value: Students choose, rehearse, and shoot film monologues with a professional cinematographer in a situation mimicking a professional shoot; monologues are edited and posted on the School website; the class also includes workshops/meetings with casting directors, agents, managers, entertainment lawyers, and actors, and ends with students shooting, examining, and reshooting audition scenes from all genres.
findings.quote: DRAM 473b, Taming the Cyclops This class begins with choosing, rehearsing for, and finally shooting film monologues. Carefully selected monologues from films or television that show the student at their best are rehearsed individually over two classes, and, with the help of a professional cinematographer and their equipment, each student's monologue is shot in a situation that mimics a professional shoot as closely as possible. The monologues are edited professionally and posted on the School website at the end of the final semester... The class also includes workshops and meetings with some of the leading professional casting directors, agents, managers, entertainment lawyers, and actors working in the industry. ... At the end of the semester, students shoot, examine, and reshoot audition scenes from all genres of film and television... Ellen Novack

findings.what: DRAM 743b Professional Preparation and Audition Workshop: description
findings.value: Addresses the social and artistic dynamics of theater auditions; students receive sides to prepare, work with a reader, make real-time adjustments, and observe each other with generosity.
findings.quote: DRAM 743b, Professional Preparation and Audition Workshop This workshop addresses the complex social and artistic dynamics of theater auditions and gives students a chance to further develop their personal practice and craft in preparation for pursuing opportunities in the field. Students receive sides to prepare, work with a reader, and are asked to make adjustments in real time, as well as to observe each other closely with generosity in an effort to develop confidence in best practices and their own individuality. Tamilla Woodard

findings.value: In their final term, students choose and rehearse scenes presented to agents, managers, casting directors, and other industry members in New York and Los Angeles; Wallace and Woodard assist in scene selection with input from Novack and an industry guest, and Mullins directs the showcase performance.
findings.quote: DRAM 793b, Actor Showcase In their final term, students choose and rehearse scenes, which are presented to agents, managers, casting directors, and other members of the industry in New York and Los Angeles. Gregory Wallace and Tamilla Woodard assist in the scene selection process with input from Ellen Novack and an industry guest. Paul Mullins directs the showcase performance. Gregory Wallace, Tamilla Woodard

findings.what: Fall 2026 orientation and registration calendar dates
findings.value: Pre-orientation training/workshops Aug. 17-21 (M-F); fall-term registration during Aug. 24-29 (M-SA); required training and orientation sessions for all students Aug. 31 (M); fall-term classes begin Sept. 7, 9 a.m.
findings.quote: Aug. 17-21  M-F   Required pre-orientation training and workshops as scheduled / Aug. 24-29  M-SA  Fall term begins / Fall-term registration for all students / Aug. 31     M     Required training and orientation sessions for all students / Sept. 7      M     Fall-term classes begin, 9 a.m.

findings.value: Students must register before fall classes begin; those who cannot attend scheduled registration need written chair permission and must notify the registrar in advance; course schedules must be submitted to the registrar within one week of the first day of classes.
findings.quote: Students must register prior to the beginning of classes in the fall. Students who cannot attend the scheduled fall-term registration must receive written permission from their program chair and notify the registrar in advance. All international students are required to complete a nonacademic registration with the Office of International Students and Scholars prior to the beginning of classes, in addition to the School's registration. All students must submit their course schedules to the registrar within one week of the first day of classes of each term and are responsible for notifying the registrar of any subsequent changes in their schedules.

findings.value: The University Theatre at 222 York Street is the School's center, a 636-seat proscenium theater shared with the undergraduate dramatic association, and also houses main administrative offices, scene/prop/metal/electrics/costume shops, a lounge, and several classrooms.
findings.source: https://bulletin.yale.edu/sites/default/files/david-geffen-school-of-drama-2026-2027.pdf (Life at the David Geffen School of Drama, Facilities)
findings.quote: The University Theatre at 222 York Street is David Geffen School of Drama at Yale's center. It includes a proscenium theater, seating 636, which is shared with the undergraduate dramatic association. The University Theatre also houses the main administrative offices; the scene, prop, metal, electrics, and costume shops; a lounge; and several classrooms.

findings.value: Yale Repertory Theatre is in a distinctive historical building, the former Calvary Baptist Church, at the corner of Chapel and York streets, containing a 479-seat auditorium facing a modified apron stage and the School/Rep box office.
findings.source: https://bulletin.yale.edu/sites/default/files/david-geffen-school-of-drama-2026-2027.pdf (Life at the David Geffen School of Drama, Facilities)
findings.quote: Yale Repertory Theatre is in a distinctive historical building on the corner of Chapel and York streets. Formerly the Calvary Baptist Church, the theater contains a 479-seat auditorium facing a modified apron stage, and the School and Yale Repertory Theatre box office.

findings.value: The Iseman Theater, in Holcombe T. Green, Jr. Hall at 1156 Chapel Street, contains a flexible performance space seating up to 200; the building also houses the Yale School of Art.
findings.source: https://bulletin.yale.edu/sites/default/files/david-geffen-school-of-drama-2026-2027.pdf (Life at the David Geffen School of Drama, Facilities)
findings.quote: The Iseman Theater in Holcombe T. Green, Jr. Hall, located at 1156 Chapel Street, contains a flexible performance space, seating up to 200. This building also houses the Yale School of Art.

findings.value: 217 Park Street contains the Yale Cabaret as well as rehearsal rooms and performance space, classrooms, faculty offices, and the offices of Theater magazine.
findings.source: https://bulletin.yale.edu/sites/default/files/david-geffen-school-of-drama-2026-2027.pdf (Life at the David Geffen School of Drama, Facilities)
findings.quote: 217 Park Street contains the Yale Cabaret as well as rehearsal rooms and performance space, classrooms, faculty offices, and the offices of Theater magazine.

findings.what: Facilities: Robert B. Haas Family Arts Library
findings.value: The Haas Family Arts Library at 180 York Street merges the former Art & Architecture and Drama Libraries, Arts of the Book Collection, and Visual Resources Collection; drama collections hold about 20,000 volumes; students may also use the three central Yale libraries.
findings.source: https://bulletin.yale.edu/sites/default/files/david-geffen-school-of-drama-2026-2027.pdf (Life at the David Geffen School of Drama, Facilities)
findings.quote: The Robert B. Haas Family Arts Library at 180 York Street encompasses the merged holdings of the former Art & Architecture and Drama Libraries, the Arts of the Book Collection, and the Visual Resources Collection. This makes it the primary collection for the study of art, architecture, and drama production at Yale. Currently, the drama collections have approximately 20,000 volumes... David Geffen School of Drama students are free to use all Yale University Library collections, including those of the three central libraries--Sterling Memorial Library, Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, and the Anne T. and Robert M. Bass Library--and of the other graduate and professional schools.

findings.value: Yale Health operates a multispecialty group practice at the Yale Health Center, 55 Lock Street; students get free, automatic primary care access through Yale Health Basic Student Health Services.
findings.source: https://bulletin.yale.edu/sites/default/files/david-geffen-school-of-drama-2026-2027.pdf (Yale University Resources and Services, Health Services)
findings.quote: Yale Health operates a multispecialty group practice on campus through its state-of-the-art medical center, Yale Health Center, located at 55 Lock Street. ... students are automatically provided with primary care services at the Yale Health Center through Yale Health Basic Student Health Services. These services are free and automatically provided; no enrollment or...

findings.value: Regular and on-time attendance at classes, production assignments, rehearsals, work-study, required workshops, and School meetings is expected and required; unexcused absences/persistent lateness are subject to disciplinary action.
findings.quote: In alignment with professional practice, regular and on-time attendance at scheduled classes, production assignments, rehearsals, work-study assignments, required workshops, and School meetings is both expected and required. Unexcused absences and/or persistent unexcused lateness are behaviors subject to disciplinary action.

findings.value: Students whose health needs, including medical appointments, require missing or being late to class should alert professors by email, copying the program chair and senior administrative assistant; students remain responsible for missed work on a schedule the professor sets.
findings.quote: Responsible self-care is the starting point for wellness and learning, and clear and timely communication supports the community's well-being. Students whose health needs, including medical appointments, require them to miss or be late for class should alert their professors by email, copying their program's chair and senior administrative assistant. Students remain responsible for the work missed, on a schedule determined by the professor.

findings.value: All casting of student actors in School or Yale Rep productions, including understudy casting, is assigned by the chair of Acting and approved by the dean, based on each student's developmental needs and the project's needs.
findings.quote: All casting of student actors in productions at the School or at Yale Repertory Theatre, including understudy casting, is assigned by the chair of Acting and approved by the dean, based on the developmental needs of each student and on the needs of the project.

findings.what: Outside performance / outside employment policy wording
findings.value: The School discourages students from pursuing outside paid or unpaid professional work while school is in session; rare short-term outside work requires a written proposal, chair review, and dean approval, with international students also needing OISS work authorization.
findings.quote: Given the collaborative nature of our work and the ongoing demands of classes and production, the School discourages students from pursuing outside paid or unpaid professional work while school is in session. In rare situations, professionally meaningful, short-term outside work that is communicated to the program chair and dean with timeliness and transparency is approved. ... Accepting and performing outside work without required approval is regarded as a conflict of interest and may lead to academic warning or dismissal.

findings.value: Rehearsals are normally scheduled 3-10 p.m. Tuesday-Friday, with Sunday normally the day off; a director may ordinarily rehearse a major School production no more than six hours in a day, and double-cast actors are ordinarily not called more than six hours a day and cannot do Yale Cabaret productions.
findings.quote: Rehearsals are normally scheduled from 3 p.m. to 10 p.m., Tuesday through Friday, with earlier start times possible on Saturdays and during technical rehearsals. Sunday is normally the day off. ... A director may ordinarily rehearse a major School production no more than six hours in one day. Actors who are double cast are ordinarily not called more than six hours a day and cannot participate in Yale Cabaret productions. The final week before the opening of a production may contain exceptions to these rules.

findings.what: First-year acting / scene study practice: official plan-of-study description
findings.value: The School's own Plan of Study page (drama.yale.edu, first-hand official source) describes the first year as a disciplined period focused on craft fundamentals (active listening, authentic response, imagination, play), with models of realism explored through scenes by contemporary/modern playwrights as actors mine the text for given circumstances, character, objective, and action while acquiring voice and speech skills. No published description of scene-partner pairing procedures, presentation format, or critique process was located.
findings.quote: The first year is a highly disciplined period of training, with a concentration on the basic principles of craft that lead to extraordinary acting: active listening, authentic response, expansive imagination, and a spirit of play. ... Models of realism are explored through work on a variety of scenes by contemporary and modern playwrights, as actors identify practical tools for mining the printed text for given circumstances, character, objective, and action while also acquiring voice and speech skills.
